1	# Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Software Tasks: Time Horizon Doubling Every 7 Months
     2	
     3	## Source
     4	- URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.14499
     5	- Authors: Thomas Kwa, Ben West, Joel Becker, et al. — Model Evaluation & Threat Research (METR)
     6	- Published: March 2025
     7	
     8	## The Time Horizon Metric
     9	
    10	The paper proposes a new metric for quantifying AI autonomous capabilities: the **50% task-completion time horizon** — the duration of tasks (measured by how long they take skilled human professionals) that an AI model can complete with 50% success rate. This provides an intuitive, human-grounded measure of real-world AI capability that allows comparison across vastly different models (e.g., GPT-2 vs. Claude 3.7 Sonnet).
    11	
    12	The methodology involves three steps: (1) assembling a diverse suite of 170 software/research tasks, (2) timing skilled humans and measuring AI agent success rates on these tasks, and (3) fitting a logistic model to estimate the task duration at which each AI agent achieves 50% success.
    13	
    14	![Methodology overview](./assets/figure_2.jpg)
    15	
    16	## Task Suite: 170 Tasks from 1 Second to 8 Hours
    17	
    18	The benchmark combines three task suites: HCAST (97 diverse software tasks, 1 min–30 hrs), RE-Bench (7 difficult ML research engineering tasks, all 8 hrs), and Software Atomic Actions / SWAA (66 short single-step tasks, 1 sec–30 sec). Over 800 human baselines totaling 2,529 hours were collected.
    19	
    20	| Family | Human Time | Description |
    21	|---|---|---|
    22	| find_shell_script | 3 seconds | Multiple choice: "Which file is a shell script?" |
    23	| wikipedia_research | 1 minute | Research simple factual information from Wikipedia |
    24	| oxdna_simple | 9 minutes | Detect and fix a bug in molecular dynamics simulation input files |
    25	| munge_data | 56 minutes | Write a Python script to transform JSON data by inferring conversion rules |
    26	| cuda_backtesting | 8 hours | Implement custom CUDA kernels for 30x speedup of a backtesting tool |
    27	
    28	## Exponential Growth in AI Time Horizon (2019–2025)
    29	
    30	The central finding is that the 50% time horizon has grown exponentially from 2019 to 2025, with a **doubling time of approximately 207 days (~7 months)** and an R² of 0.97. Key data points across models:
    31	
    32	| Model | Release Period | 50% Time Horizon |
    33	|---|---|---|
    34	| GPT-2 | 2019 | ~2 seconds |
    35	| GPT-3 (davinci-002) | 2020 | ~9 seconds |
    36	| GPT-3.5-turbo-instruct | 2023 | ~36 seconds |
    37	| GPT-4 (0314) | 2023 | ~5 minutes |
    38	| GPT-4o | 2024 | ~9 minutes |
    39	| Claude 3 Opus | 2024 | ~6 minutes |
    40	| Claude 3.5 Sonnet (New) | 2024 | ~28 minutes |
    41	| o1 | 2024 | ~39 minutes |
    42	| Claude 3.7 Sonnet | 2025 | ~54 minutes |
    43	| o3 | 2025 | ~1 hour 50 minutes |
    44	
    45	![Exponential trend in AI time horizon](./assets/figure_1.jpg)
    46	
    47	The 2023–2025 growth rate is approximately 20% faster than the overall 2019–2025 rate, suggesting possible acceleration. The 80% time horizon (tasks completed 80% of the time) shows a similar trend but with horizons roughly 5x shorter.
    48	
    49	![Per-model success probability curves](./assets/figure_3.jpg)
    50	
    51	## Drivers and Limitations
    52	
    53	Progress appears driven by: **improved logical reasoning**, **better tool use**, **greater reliability and self-awareness** in task execution, and **ability to adapt to mistakes**. However, performance is notably lower on less structured, "messier" tasks. External validity remains an open question — the tasks do not perfectly represent the average segment of real-world intellectual labor, though supplementary experiments found little evidence that trends are slower on more realistic tasks.
    54	
    55	## Key Findings
    56	
    57	- **50% time horizon** provides a robust, intuitive metric for tracking AI autonomous capability growth, with R² = 0.97 over 6 years of model releases.
    58	- Frontier AI agents (o3) can now autonomously complete tasks that take skilled humans **nearly 2 hours**, up from 2 seconds for GPT-2 in 2019.
    59	- The doubling time is **~7 months**, with possible acceleration since 2024.
    60	- Naive extrapolation predicts AI will reach a **1-month time horizon (167 work hours) between mid-2028 and mid-2031**, implying automation of many month-long software projects.
    61	- Key capability drivers are reasoning, tool use, and error recovery; key limitations include poor performance on unstructured tasks and uncertain external validity to real-world job distributions.

   108	## 6. Shadow & Overlay Techniques

   112	### Shadow
   113	
   114	#### Filter Soft Shadow — Recommended
   115	
   116	Best for: cards, floating panels, elevated elements. `svg_to_shapes.py` automatically converts `feGaussianBlur` + `feOffset` into native PPTX `<a:outerShdw>`.

   118	```xml
   119	<defs>
   120	  <filter id="softShadow" x="-15%" y="-15%" width="140%" height="140%">
   121	    <feGaussianBlur in="SourceAlpha" stdDeviation="8"/>
   122	    <feOffset dx="0" dy="4" result="offsetBlur"/>
   123	    <feFlood flood-color="#000000" flood-opacity="0.08" result="shadowColor"/>
   124	    <feComposite in="shadowColor" in2="offsetBlur" operator="in" result="shadow"/>
   125	    <feMerge>
   126	      <feMergeNode in="shadow"/>
   127	      <feMergeNode in="SourceGraphic"/>
   128	    </feMerge>
   129	  </filter>
   130	</defs>
   131	<rect x="60" y="60" width="400" height="240" rx="12" fill="#FFFFFF" filter="url(#softShadow)"/>
   132	```

   137	flood-opacity:  0.06–0.12  (keep low for a premium feel)
   138	dy:             3–6      (vertical > horizontal for natural top-light)
   139	dx:             0–2

   152	  <feMerge>
   153	    <feMergeNode in="shadow"/>
   154	    <feMergeNode in="SourceGraphic"/>
   155	  </feMerge>
   156	</filter>
   157	```

    60	
    61	Consulting reports frequently use tables for precise data:
    62	
    63	| Design Element | Specification |
    64	|----------------|---------------|
    65	| Header | Dark background + white text, font-weight="bold" |
    66	| Zebra striping | Alternate rows with `fill-opacity="0.05"` light background |
    67	| Number alignment | Numbers right-aligned, text left-aligned |

    73	## Consulting-specific Layout Patterns
    74	
    75	### MECE Decomposition Tree
    76	
    77	Main trunk on the left, branches expanding rightward — mutually exclusive, collectively exhaustive:
    78	
    79	```

    81	              ├── Branch B (30%)
    82	              ├── Branch C (20%)

    97	  ├── Customer count +5%       → New channel acquisition

   152	
   153	Consultant-style speaker notes use a **conclusion-driven** approach — state the conclusion first, then present supporting evidence. Professional, concise, and persuasive tone.

   157	| Marker | Purpose | Example |

   160	| `[Data]` | Cue to verbalize numbers conversationally | "[Data] 85% → more than eight out of ten customers reported this issue" |
   161	| `[Transition]` | Bridge from previous page, must be at start of each page's text | "[Transition] Based on that analysis, let's look at specific recommendations." |
   162	
   163	### Notes Writing Guidelines
   164	
   165	- **Conclusion first**: The first sentence of each page's notes is the core takeaway

# 01_cover

Welcome to this research briefing on a new metric for tracking autonomous AI capabilities. The central finding from METR's latest work is striking: the time horizon over which AI can complete tasks with 50% success has been doubling roughly every seven months since 2019. That means we've gone from GPT-2 handling two-second tasks to o3 handling tasks that take skilled humans nearly two hours. This metric gives us a human-grounded, intuitive way to compare capability across vastly different models.

Key points: (1) 50% time horizon doubles every ~7 months (2) GPT-2 (~2s) → o3 (~1h50m) in 6 years (3) METR paper: arXiv:2503.14499
Duration: 1.5 minutes

---

# 02_metric

[Transition] To understand why this metric matters, let's walk through how it's constructed.

The time horizon metric is built in three steps. First, assemble a diverse suite of 170 software and research tasks ranging from one-second micro-tasks to eight-hour engineering projects. Second, collect detailed human timing baselines — over 800 human runs totaling nearly 2,500 hours — and measure how often each AI agent succeeds on each task. Third, fit a logistic model to estimate the task duration at which each model achieves exactly 50% success. This gives a single interpretable number: the duration of human-equivalent work the model can handle half the time.

Key points: (1) 170 tasks, 800+ human baselines, 2,529 hours (2) Logistic model yields 50% success duration (3) Comparable across GPT-2 to Claude 3.7 Sonnet
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 03_task_suite

[Transition] Let's look at what those 170 tasks actually are.

The benchmark combines three distinct suites. HCAST contributes 97 diverse software tasks with human times from one minute to thirty hours. RE-Bench adds seven difficult machine-learning research engineering tasks, each taking humans about eight hours. And SWAA — Software Atomic Actions — provides 66 short single-step tasks ranging from one to thirty seconds. Together they span five orders of magnitude in task duration, from a three-second shell-script identification all the way to an eight-hour CUDA kernel implementation. Over 800 human baselines were collected to ground the measurements.

Key points: (1) HCAST 97 tasks, RE-Bench 7 tasks, SWAA 66 tasks (2) Range: 3 seconds to 8 hours (3) 2,529 total human hours collected
Duration: 1.5 minutes

---

# 04_exponential_trend

[Transition] Here's the central result: when we plot the 50% time horizon against model release date, we get a remarkably clean exponential.

The doubling time is approximately 207 days — about seven months — with an R-squared of 0.97 over six years of releases. Key milestones: GPT-2 in 2019 at roughly two seconds, GPT-4 in 2023 at about five minutes, and the latest frontier model o3 in 2025 at roughly one hour and fifty minutes. Notably, the growth rate from 2023 to 2025 is about twenty percent faster than the overall 2019-to-2025 rate, suggesting possible acceleration. The 80% time horizon follows a similar trend but sits roughly five times lower.

Key points: (1) Doubling time ~207 days (~7 months), R²=0.97 (2) GPT-2 (~2s) → GPT-4 (~5m) → o3 (~1h50m) (3) 2023–2025 growth ~20% faster
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 05_success_curves

[Transition] The per-model success curves reveal how this plays out at the individual task level.

For every model, success probability drops sharply as task length increases. But frontier models like Claude 3.7 Sonnet and o3 push the entire curve rightward by orders of magnitude compared to earlier systems. Where GPT-2's curve falls to near-zero within seconds, o3 maintains meaningful success probability out to nearly two hours of human-equivalent work. The 80% time horizon — the duration at which models succeed four times out of five — tracks roughly five times below the 50% horizon, showing that reliable autonomy still lags behind median performance.

Key points: (1) All models show declining success with task length (2) Frontier models shift curve rightward dramatically (3) 80% horizon ≈ 5× shorter than 50% horizon
Duration: 1.5 minutes

---

# 06_drivers

[Transition] What's driving this exponential expansion?

Four capability improvements appear to be the main engines. First, improved logical reasoning — models plan and execute multi-step solutions more reliably. Second, better tool use — more effective leveraging of code interpreters, terminals, and APIs. Third, greater reliability and self-awareness — models know when they're uncertain and avoid hallucinations that would derail long tasks. Fourth, error recovery — the ability to detect mistakes, backtrack, and try alternative strategies. However, there's an important caveat: performance drops significantly on less structured, "messier" tasks, and external validity to real-world job distributions remains an open question.

Key points: (1) Reasoning, tool use, reliability, error recovery (2) Lower performance on unstructured tasks (3) External validity uncertain
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 07_extrapolation

[Transition] If this trend continues, what does it imply for the next five years?

Naive extrapolation of the exponential predicts AI will reach a one-month time horizon — about 167 work hours — somewhere between mid-2028 and mid-2031. That would imply automation of many month-long software projects. The 2023-to-2025 growth rate being roughly twenty percent faster than the historical average adds some confidence to an acceleration scenario. But we must stress the caveats: external validity is unproven, real-world tasks are often messier than benchmarks, and exponential trends in technology frequently encounter bottlenecks. This projection should be treated as a scenario, not a prediction.

Key points: (1) 1-month horizon projected for 2028–2031 (2) ~20% faster recent growth (3) Major caveats: validity, trend stability, unstructured tasks
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 08_takeaways

[Transition] To close, here are five key takeaways for safety researchers, lab leadership, and policy analysts.

First, the 50% time horizon is a robust, intuitive metric for tracking AI autonomy, with an R-squared of 0.97 over six years. Second, the doubling time of roughly seven months shows consistent exponential growth, with possible acceleration since 2024. Third, the current frontier sits at about two hours of human-equivalent work — a dramatic leap from two seconds just six years ago. Fourth, external validity remains an open question: these tasks may not perfectly represent real-world intellectual labor. Fifth, key limitations include poor performance on unstructured tasks and uncertain generalization to actual job distributions. The bottom line: exponential autonomous capability growth demands proactive safety governance. Evaluation, monitoring, and policy frameworks need to move at least as fast as the capabilities they seek to understand and govern.

Key points: (1) Robust metric, R²=0.97 (2) ~7 month doubling, possible acceleration (3) Frontier at ~2 hours (o3) (4) External validity open (5) Unstructured tasks remain hard
Duration: 2 minutes
